title: Bridget of Sweden (1303–1373)
hookLine: mother of eight, widow, founder, co-patron of Europe

lines: A HOUSEFUL OF CHILDREN, NOW GROWN.
cards: A fresh grave at a monastery in Sweden. The widow standing beside it was married young.
She has raised a houseful of children, run an estate, served at the royal court, and walked a long pilgrimage road beside her husband, Ulf. Now Ulf is buried, and the life she knew is over.
The expected next chapter is a quiet one: a chair by the fire, grandchildren, prayers. Instead, she begins again, in a new country, with a new work and a voice that reaches popes.

teach.b: Start with the first life. Bridget was born into a noble family and married young.
Tradition remembers her as a mother who prayed with her children and fed the poor at her own door, and one of her daughters, Catherine, is honored as a saint too. Next, the turn.

teach.h: WIDOWED, SHE GIVES HERSELF TO PRAYER.
teach.b: After Ulf died, Bridget gave away much of what she had and gave herself to prayer. She wrote down visions, later gathered as her Revelations, many of them meditations on the suffering of Christ.
The Church is careful here. The Catechism says private revelations don't add to the faith; they can help people live it, and they're weighed, not required. Then, the new work.

teach.h: AN ORDER FOUNDED, A LIFE IN ROME.
teach.b: Bridget founded the Order of the Most Holy Savior, under a rule she wrote. And she went to Rome, and stayed.

The popes of her day lived at Avignon, in France, and Bridget, years before Catherine of Siena, wrote to them plainly, urging them home to Rome. She didn't live to see it settled; yesterday's schism came after her.
The Church has named Bridget a co-patron of Europe, beside Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein.
A woman who crossed the continent on pilgrim roads, from the far north to Rome and on to the Holy Land, now stands for the whole of it.
Paul's first letter to Timothy describes a widow who trusts in God and keeps praying, night and day. Bridget did that, then got up and went to work.
A second life can be larger than the first.

how: Catholics keep Saint Bridget's feast in the calendar, and the order she founded, the Bridgettines, still lives and prays in houses in several countries. Some Catholics pray for Europe on her feast and on the feasts of its other patron saints.

o: a Swedish queen who brought the faith to the north
a widow who founded an order and urged popes home
an abbess who wrote the rule for Benedictine nuns

games.q: you're Bridget. your husband has just died, your children are grown, and you have money, rank and a quiet house. what do you do?
o: stay home and live a quiet, comfortable widowhood.
remarry and keep your place at court.
give much of it away, found an order, and go to Rome.
games.why: she gave herself to prayer, founded an order, moved to Rome, and wrote plainly to popes. her second life reached further than her first.

practice: Picture the roads Bridget walked, north to south, cold coasts, mountain passes, crowded cities, or one country in Europe you know or have family in, and let a few faces come: a family just arrived somewhere new, a parish choir, a teenager on a night train.
If you pray, ask Bridget's prayers for them or pray an Our Father with that place in mind; if not, hold it the way you'd hold a friend's name.

wordCard.voice: Bridget. A noble wife and mother who, once widowed, founded an order, moved to Rome, and spoke plainly to popes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a widow's second life. Loss closed one door for Bridget, and she walked through another. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.
